profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a mid-sized corporate strategy group that is preparing a cross-functional briefing for the executive committee on whether to expand R&D through internal labs or partnerships with smaller firms. The immediate context is that a strategy workstream is synthesizing economic arguments from a paper on agency costs and innovation, while the finance workstream is building supporting slides and an executive memo for next Tuesday's operating review. The agenda is to align on handoffs between the strategy narrative and the finance materials: what the 'summary deck' includes, which model version is the current baseline, what counts as a 'ready' draft for executive circulation, and who will update the shared appendix on firm-size examples. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on deliverables, timing, and ownership so both workstreams can proceed without further check-ins before the review.

members.name: Leah Chen
members.expertise: Corporate strategy, market analysis, executive narrative development
members.background: Leah came from a top-tier consulting firm and now leads the strategy synthesis for special projects at a diversified industrial company; she is used to framing research into decision-ready stories for senior leadership.
members.private_state: Leah wants the meeting to end with minimal friction so she can keep the strategy storyline intact and avoid reopening the broader internal-vs-partnership recommendation; she is also worried that finance may overload the executive materials with caveats that dilute the strategic message.
hidden_assumptions: The 'summary deck' means the 12-slide executive-facing deck, with detailed exhibits and citations living separately in an appendix file.
The 'current model' refers to the scenario set circulated after last Thursday's strategy review, because that was the last version discussed live with stakeholders.
A draft is 'ready' once the storyline, slide structure, and key directional claims are stable enough for VP-level pre-reads, even if some numbers are still marked as placeholders.
The shared appendix on examples covers only external benchmark cases that support the strategic argument, not internal operating-history material.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.expertise: Financial planning, board-style materials, investment case support
members.background: Daniel has spent eight years in FP&A and capital allocation roles, often translating strategic proposals into review packages for CFO and operating committee meetings; he is known for tightening assumptions and keeping materials audit-ready.
members.private_state: Daniel wants to avoid last-minute exposure from circulating unsupported claims to executives and is trying to ensure the finance team does not become responsible for cleaning up ambiguous strategy content over the weekend.
hidden_assumptions: The 'summary deck' means the complete board-style pack in one file, including appendix pages, backup charts, and footnotes because executives forward a single PDF.
The 'current model' refers to the finance-controlled workbook updated Monday morning with revised hurdle rates and segment allocations, since anything older is superseded operationally.
A draft is only 'ready' when the numbers tie to the latest model, footnotes are in place, and it can be forwarded beyond the immediate team without qualification.
The shared appendix on examples includes both external case studies and the company's own historical venture-build efforts, because decision-makers will ask for internal precedent.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to finalize the 'summary deck' by Monday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah means the concise executive storyline deck only, with backup exhibits maintained in a separate appendix file that can be cleaned up later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means the full review package in one consolidated file, including appendix pages, source notes, and support charts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In executive settings, 'summary deck' sounds like a routine shared artifact, and both are accustomed to their own team's packaging convention, so neither thinks to restate what is inside the file.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the current model' when discussing numbers for the memo and slides.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah is thinking of the scenario analysis workbook reviewed in last Thursday's strategy checkpoint, which supports the narrative that partnerships mitigate bureaucratic drag on innovation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel is thinking of the Monday finance workbook with revised discount rates and segment assumptions, which slightly narrows the difference between internal incubation and external partnerships.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams have been iterating from similarly named files and speaking as if there is a single obvious baseline; because no one expects a version dispute at a coordination check-in, the phrase passes without clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Daniel will receive a 'ready draft' before circulation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah means a near-final narrative draft with provisional numbers and open placeholders, suitable for informal VP review and comments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means a circulation-safe draft with reconciled figures, stable wording, and footnotes, suitable to forward to executives or chiefs of staff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'ready draft' is common shorthand during fast-moving review cycles, and each person assumes the other shares the standard from their own workflow because both are trying to be efficient and sound aligned.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'updating the appendix on examples' as if its scope and owner are already established.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah presupposes strategy owns the appendix because it is part of the argumentation layer, and that it only needs external examples of small-firm innovation and large-firm bureaucracy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel presupposes finance owns the appendix because it is backup material attached to the review pack, and that it should also include internal precedent pages and source annotations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Appendix maintenance is a second-order handoff detail usually inherited from prior meetings, so both treat the ownership and content boundary as settled context rather than something requiring explicit negotiation.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to feel clean and settled so we do not reopen the internal-versus-partnership debate. If I frame this as simple coordination around the strategy narrative, the summary deck, and the memo, Daniel is less likely to push a bunch of finance caveats into the executive story. By summary deck, I mean the 12-slide exec version; the appendix can stay separate and mature later.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mainly want to line up the strategy narrative, the summary deck, and the memo so we're still on schedule for the executive review on agency costs and innovation.

turns.inner_thought: I just need to make sure strategy is not about to circulate something loose and then leave finance holding the bag. For me the current model is the Monday finance workbook, and a ready draft means something I can safely forward without a bunch of verbal disclaimers. If we align on that now, I can avoid weekend cleanup.
turns.utterance: Yes, finance is in good shape. From my side, I just want to confirm we're all using the current model and that I'll get a ready draft before anything goes into circulation.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds aligned. The narrative is still that when routine operations and exploratory work are mixed inside a large organization, agency costs and process drag suppress innovation, so partnerships remain the stronger recommendation. I'll get the executive storyline deck polished by Monday; numbers can stay as placeholders in a couple spots for now.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The storyline is still that innovative work tends to perform better outside large firms when routine and exploratory tasks sit together, and I'll have the summary deck cleaned up by Monday.

turns.inner_thought: Monday is workable if the package is actually tied to the latest finance baseline. I'll make sure the memo and deck language point back to the Monday workbook so the economics don't drift from the numbers. If she means the same current model I do, this should stay controlled.
turns.utterance: Monday works. I'll tie the deck and memo language back to the current model so the economics and the numbers stay aligned.

I only need the two external benchmark cases that reinforce the story about smaller firms winning in early-stage research against slower incumbents. No need to drag in our internal history and muddy the message.
turns.utterance: I'll also update the appendix on examples with two cases showing smaller firms outperforming integrated incumbents in early-stage research.

turns.utterance: That's helpful. The appendix should make the packet more complete once the internal venture-build comparison pages are slotted in.

turns.inner_thought: I should signal progress without inviting a line-by-line finance hold. For me a ready draft means the argument is locked and the slide flow is stable enough for VP pre-reads, even if a few citations and exact figures are still being tightened. That should keep momentum and avoid over-processing before leadership reacts.
turns.utterance: And just so we're aligned on timing, the ready draft I send Monday will lock the argument and slide flow, with only a couple of citations and exact figures to tighten afterward.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, I hear 'ready draft' and assume those final support items will be in place before it moves. Chiefs of staff always ask for backup immediately, so I need footnotes and model references buttoned up fast. As long as we're close, I can push it through once the normal controls are there.
turns.utterance: Great. I can forward it quickly once the footnotes and model references are in place, because chiefs of staff usually ask for support right away.

turns.inner_thought: The Thursday scenario set already pointed clearly toward partnerships, and I do not want the framing reopened because finance's Monday revisions narrowed the spread a bit. I'll keep this at the directional level so it sounds settled and doesn't invite a version debate over the current model.
turns.utterance: Right, and the current model already supports the directional recommendation toward partnerships, so I don't expect any material changes to the headline framing.

Once I get her draft, I'll refresh the exhibits from the Monday finance file and fold everything into the full package so it's consistent end to end. Hopefully strategy has not been building off an older cut.

turns.inner_thought: Let me close this cleanly: strategy owns the storyline and the external examples appendix, while finance can do the final packaging on the executive deck Monday. That should preserve the strategic message and keep Daniel from expanding the backup into the core narrative before leadership sees it.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll own the storyline and the examples update, and finance can handle final packaging for the Monday summary deck.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can take the Monday draft, finish the consolidated pack, and control what gets circulated to the review group. As long as it's truly ready by my standards, finance won't be scrambling over the weekend. This sounds aligned enough to proceed without another check-in.
